economics._method: Cash-recovery basis, no depreciation. floor_Nm = (capex_per_gpu / N + cash_opex_per_installed_hour * 744) / (730 * occupancy). Occupancy default 0.75 (a sensitivity assumption, not current PAYG utilisation). Payback at a price p and occupancy u = capex_per_gpu / (p * 730 * u - cash_opex_per_installed_hour * 744) months. GB200 / GB300 / VR are not in the portfolio workbook (no PAYG); only the SemiAnalysis modeled cost floor exists for them.

perf._source: Delivered-performance multiples between GPU generations, assembled 2026-09-15 from MLCommons results, NVIDIA/Nebius/Lambda/StorageReview MLPerf write-ups, SemiAnalysis InferenceX (VR) and the GB300 pricing template's validated evidence; independently verified the same day (all ratios re-derived; no base moved by more than 15%).
perf._method: base = customer-realisable multiple = 1 + 0.75 x (raw per-GPU ratio - 1), raw = blend of same-round MLPerf training and inference per-GPU ratios; low = weakest measured leg; high = vendor dense-TFLOPS ratio (or the raw measured peak where no spec ratio applies). The parity ceiling uses base; the page lets the user override it.

_realisation_factor.rationale: The template's ratified bridge (sku-pricing-template-spec.md:23: raw ratio x0.75 customer realisation x substitute price = term ceiling) is kept at 0.75 but applied to the UPLIFT, realised = 1 + 0.75 x (raw - 1), not to the raw ratio: on the big Hopper-to-Blackwell jumps the two conventions differ by ~0.1-0.4x (GB300/H200 3.36 vs 3.5), while on the 1.07-1.17x intra-generation steps multiplying the raw ratio by 0.75 would assert the newer chip is SLOWER (1.068 x 0.75 = 0.80), which no data supports. Why 0.75 and not 1.0: (1) precision mix - the headline MLPerf ratios put NVFP4 on the new part against FP8 on the old; a customer who stays FP8/BF16 sees the dense FP8 spec gap (B200/H100 2.27x vs 3-4x measured; GB300/H200 2.5x vs 4.7-5.2x), and Nebius' reserve book is still majority FP8/BF16 training; (2) closed-division MLPerf is vendor-tuned peak and open-source stacks trail by months - GB300's own day-0 numbers were 36-60% of its 6-months-later numbers (DSR1 server 2,907->8,064, offline 5,842->9,821), so a launch-quarter customer realises materially less than the later lab figure; (3) fragmentation and idle time do not shrink with per-GPU throughput, so cost-per-unit-of-work improves less than tokens/s; (4) the only day-0 realisation actually measured on a new part is VR at ~61% of dense spec (build_vr_v2.py:9), which brackets 0.75 from below. Why not lower: for mature pairs (H200/H100, B300/B200, GB300/B300) both sides are on the same precision and the same software generation, so the uplift is nearly fully realised - applying 0.75 to the uplift only costs 2-6 points there, which is the right order. Blend: base = arithmetic mean of central training raw and central inference raw (50/50) reflecting the mixed reserve book; VR is inference-only because no training measurement exists.

_caveats: Hopper baseline in the GB300-vs-H200 4.7x/5.2x figure is NVIDIA-internal ('not verified by MLCommons Association') and mixes NVFP4 vs FP8 - the MLCommons-verified chains give 3.7-5.4x; the base 3.36 already discounts this.

VR is pre-release: only SemiAnalysis single-rack per-MW measurements (Jul-26 and 14-Sep-26, early software) and vendor specs exist; no MLPerf entry; no training measurement at all, so VR base is inference-only and the 50/50 blend rule could not be applied. Re-check at the next MLPerf Inference round (~Sep-Oct 2026) and at RFS; template trigger: step down if <1.8x measured.

Per-MW vs per-GPU: SemiAnalysis normalises VR per all-in utility MW; at 190-230 kW vs 132-142 kW rack power the per-GPU multiple is ~1.35-1.7x higher than the per-MW one (2.0 -> ~2.7-3.5 at 100 TPS). Kept 2.0 as base because it is one pre-production rack on pre-release software; flag as the single biggest swing in the VR ceiling.

Training-side multiples for Blackwell vs Hopper come from different rounds (B200 v4.1 at FP8; GB200 v5.0 vs v5.1 with NVFP4 training added) - software ramp is confounded with hardware; I used the earlier, FP8-era numbers for HGX B200 (2.0-2.2x vs H100) and the same-GPU-count v5.1 statements for GB300.

GB200-vs-B200 and GB300-vs-B300 have no equal-scale training pair; their training centrals (1.10 / 1.08) are spec-and-memory inferences, not measurements. Aggregated inference shows per-GPU parity (0.93-1.03x); the NVL72 value is workload-conditional (disaggregated interactive +47%, rack-scale MoE serving +106-263% per InferenceX) and should be priced as a workload premium rather than a chip multiple.
H200-vs-H100 'high' is the raw measured 1.5x, not a vendor dense-TFLOPS ratio, because FP8 dense compute is identical (1,979 TFLOPS); NVIDIA's marketed 1.9x/1.6x claims are excluded.

Nebius v6.0 and Lambda v6.0 per-GPU numbers were read from vendor blogs, not re-derived from the MLCommons results tables; the GB300 v5.1 numbers (5,842 / 2,907) were cross-checked exact against the template's MLCommons-validated 2026-08-16/17 audit (build_final_v4.py:746-747, memory: gb300-performance-tab-validation).

Software ramp cuts the other way for a fixed-price term: GB300 gained 2.77x server / 1.68x offline in six months on unchanged hardware (v5.1->v6.0); a 12-36 month parity ceiling priced on day-0 realisation is conservative by that amount (Value curve tab, build_final_v4.py:739-749).

Vendor dense spec ratios used for 'high': H100/H200 FP8 dense 1.979 PF; HGX B200 FP4 dense 9 PF; HGX B300 13.5 PF; GB200 10 PF; GB300 15 PF; Rubin 35 PF dense NVFP4 (50 PF sparsity-assisted), 17.5 PF FP8 dense vs GB300 5 PF. The nvidia.com GB300 page extraction returned garbled per-GPU numbers (150/75 PF); the 15 PF dense figure is taken from NVIDIA's Training v5.1 blog ('15 petaflops of NVFP4') and the '1.5x dense FP4 vs Blackwell' statement.
